fields.title: Polka: a payment about which nothing is known
fields.summary: 210 tickets for "money charged, no order" and 74 for "charged twice" in a month.
fields.decisionPrompt: What do we do in the next two weeks? Name the cost of your decision.
fields.brief/company: Polka is a fictional grocery delivery service from local stores: 900 partner stores, a customer app, and a partner portal.
fields.brief/context: You are a product manager at Polka. For the second month, the payment provider is responding slowly during evening peak hours: the median is 1.2 seconds, p95 is 14 seconds, and about 3% of requests time out. Over the month, support received 210 tickets stating "money deducted, no order" and 74 tickets stating "charged twice".
fields.brief/objective: Make retries safe and stop losing user money when the provider times out.
fields.brief/constraints: Two weeks. The provider responds within its SLA, switching takes three months.
fields.brief/task: Decide what you do in the next two weeks and name what remains unresolved.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: A retry is safe only with an idempotency key
fields.learnTakeaway/body: The network drops answers, people close the app and try again—this is normal, not an exception. An idempotency key makes retries harmless, and without it, any improvement on top leaves double charges possible. The second mandatory piece is status checking: if you cannot ask the provider how your call ended, you don't know what to show the user.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content: Checkout is synchronous: create order, call provider, wait up to 30 seconds for a response, mark as paid. No idempotency key. Button is blocked on the client.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content: "Duplicates come from people who close the app and check out again: button blocking doesn't save you, a second attempt is a new request. The provider supports an idempotency key, we don't use it. They have a payment status check method and webhooks, we connected neither."
fields.evidenceCards/2/content: Drop-off on the payment screen is 6% in calm times, 19% during evening peak. Average check is 2,400 rubles.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content: In response to slow replies, they say they operate within their SLA—p95 up to 15 seconds. Switching to another provider takes three months and reconnecting all payment methods from scratch.
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: A week and a half. The key lives from the moment the payment screen opens; on timeout—three retries, then background status reconciliation and user notification.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence: duplicates disappear almost entirely. "No order" turns into "checking, we'll send a notification." Waiting for the user remains long—up to 14 seconds at peak, drop-off will persist.
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: Three weeks. The order is created immediately in "processing payment" status, the screen is freed, the result arrives via notification. A webhook from the provider confirms payment.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence: waiting disappears, drop-off should drop. The user leaves the screen without knowing if it's paid—some people will worry and call. Requires an idempotency key anyway. Three weeks vs. two stated.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence: eliminates the root cause. Solves nothing in the quarter horizon, and duplicates continue the whole time. The new provider might also lag if we lack idempotency.
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: One week. Text changes as the wait continues, after 10 seconds "checking status, do not close", a "minimize" button with a promise of notification.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence: cheap and fast, reduces some repeat checkouts. Does not eliminate duplicates technically—the person can still close and check out again. Does not speed things up.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Does not understand why a retry is unsafe without a key
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Does not single out timeout as a distinct state
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: Failed to design an intermediate state
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: Synchronous waiting for someone else's response is not treated as a product decision
